What did the ads do, how soon could we tell, and who should see them?¶

Notes on the Criteo Uplift v2.1 experiment¶

Vangelis Gkiastas · github.com/egkiastas/incrementality-lab

All numbers below are read from report/results/*.json, written by the scripts in analysis/.

Summary for the product team¶

The ads work. Site visits go up by about 19% (+0.75 visits per 100 users) and purchases by about 48% (+0.10 per 100 users).

The usual dashboard number is too high. A straight treated-vs-held-out comparison says +27% on visits. Part of that comes from how the dataset was put together, not from the ads (section 3). Report the adjusted figure.

Most of the value sits with a small group. Showing ads to the 10% of users the uplift model ranks highest delivers 79% of the extra visits that showing them to everyone would: 6,012 per million users, against 5,082 if we pick "people likely to visit" and 758 at random. Above roughly 20% of users, the simple "likely to visit" ranking does just as well.

Nobody is put off by the ads, but half of the users barely respond. The lower-ranked half produces only about 5% of the extra visits, which makes it the obvious place to save budget.

Purchases are too rare (about 3 per 1,000 users) to target better than the simple model does.

On running tests: checking a normal A/B test after every batch of users and stopping when it looks good produced a false win in 38% of no-effect tests. The always-valid test stayed at 3%.

Recommendations:

  1. Keep the channel and concentrate spend on the top 10-20% by predicted uplift.
  2. Stop spending on the lowest-ranked half.
  3. Report the adjusted lift.
  4. Use always-valid monitoring on live tests.
  5. Consider a 50/50 split next time: it needs about half the users of 85/15 for the same certainty.

The public data was altered on purpose to hide the original campaign size, so the exact percentages won't transfer. The direction and the targeting advice should.

1. Data¶

Criteo Uplift Prediction Dataset v2.1 (Diemert et al., 2021): 13,979,592 users, 11,882,655 of them eligible to see ads. The outcomes are a visit to the advertiser's site (4.70%) and a purchase (0.292%). Only 3.6% of eligible users actually saw an ad, and control users never did. Twelve anonymised features were logged before assignment.

Two details from Criteo's paper end up mattering. The file pools several tests, each re-sampled to 85% treated, and negatives were down-sampled non-uniformly "so that the original incrementality level cannot be deduced".

2. Is the randomization clean?¶

Every standard check passes. The sample-ratio test gives p = 0.999, the largest standardized mean difference is 0.049, and 1,000 A/A splits of the control group produce false positives at 4.6% (visits) and 4.9% (conversions).

At this sample size, though, passing a threshold isn't the same as being random. The SE of an SMD under randomization is 0.00075, and 12 of 12 features are significantly imbalanced after Bonferroni. A LightGBM classifier predicts treatment with AUC 0.5073 [0.5057, 0.5089]. The treated share is also suspiciously exact: a genuine Bernoulli(0.85) assignment lands this close to 85% with probability 0.0011.

3. The average effect¶

The plain difference in means puts the visit effect at 1.034 pp [1.006, 1.063] (27.1% relative) and the conversion effect at 0.115 pp (59.4%). The exact binomial bootstrap gives [1.007, 1.063] for visits, the same as the delta method to the third decimal.

On a clean RCT, adjusting for pre-treatment features should leave the estimate where it is and only narrow the interval. Here it moves it a long way:

Estimator Visits, pp [95% CI] (shift) Conversions, pp [95% CI] (shift)
Difference in means 1.034 [1.006, 1.063] 0.115 [0.108, 0.122]
CUPED (12 features) 0.698 [0.673, 0.723] (-23 SE) 0.092 [0.085, 0.098] (-7 SE)
CUPAC (cross-fitted GBM) 0.634 [0.610, 0.658] (-27 SE) 0.090 [0.083, 0.096] (-7 SE)
Post-stratified (20 strata) 0.691 [0.665, 0.716] (-23 SE) 0.088 [0.080, 0.095] (-8 SE)
AIPW, design propensity 0.739 [0.716, 0.763] (-20 SE) 0.101 [0.095, 0.108] (-4 SE)
AIPW, estimated propensity 0.750 [0.725, 0.776] (-19 SE) 0.099 [0.093, 0.106] (-5 SE)

The figure below shows why. Sorting users by a treatment-blind prediction of visiting, the treated share rises from 84.9% in the lowest ventile to 86.5% in the highest, and those are the users with a 46.6% visit rate even without ads. Part of the raw difference is just measuring who ended up treated. Down-sampling negatives and then forcing each sub-test back to 85% would produce this.

The adjustment itself is not the problem. On 500 fake 85/15 splits of control users, the mean CUPAC estimate was 0.0001 pp (MC SE 0.0013) with a 3.8% false-positive rate.

I use AIPW with an estimated propensity as the headline: 0.750 pp [0.725, 0.776] for visits (18.6%) and 0.0995 pp for conversions (48.4%). It is consistent if either the outcome or the propensity model is right. The estimators still disagree among themselves, so the honest answer for visits is roughly 0.63-0.75 pp. These are effects in the re-sampled file.

What does actually seeing an ad do?¶

Because control users can never be exposed, assignment is an instrument for exposure (first-stage F = 444,220). Under the exclusion restriction, the Wald ratio gives the effect on users who were exposed: 28.7 pp [27.9, 29.5] on visits and 3.20 pp on conversions. Comparing exposed with unexposed users instead gives 1.32x and 1.64x those numbers, because exposed users are a selected group: their features differ by up to 1.47 SDs, and they would have visited at 12.8% with no ad at all, against 3.8% for an average control user. The IV number inherits the imbalance above (it is ITT divided by the exposure rate) and only describes the kind of user who gets exposed.

4. Variance reduction¶

There is no pre-period outcome, so the features stand in for the CUPED covariate. CUPAC replaces them with a single out-of-fold, treatment-blind LightGBM prediction (AUC 0.947 for visits). On visits CUPED removes 25% of the variance and CUPAC 31%, which is like running the plain test with 1.44x the users. On conversions the gains are 11% and 12%.

5. How soon can we tell?¶

To simulate data arriving over time, each of 1,000 A/A experiments takes 500,000 control users in random order, gives them fake 85/15 labels and looks at the data 100 times. A t-test at every look declares a winner in 37.9% of runs for visits and 37.7% for conversions. A single test at the end is at 5.9% and 6.2%. The mixture SPRT (τ = 10% of the baseline rate, decided before looking) stays at 3.0% and 0.9%.

Replaying the real experiment in 100 random arrival orders, the mSPRT called the visit effect after a median of 30,846 users (P10-P90 15,312 to 54,969) and the conversion effect after 222,879, always with the right sign. A fixed-horizon test with 80% power, sized as if you already knew the effect, would need 21,145 and 89,724. That 1.5-2.5x is the price of being allowed to look whenever you like.

The 85/15 split costs too: for the same precision it needs 1.96x the users of a 50/50 split. Simulating the power formula at its own MDE gave 79.3% power against the 80% target.

6. Who responds?¶

I split all users once, stratified on treatment and visit: 60% train, 10% validation and 30% test (4,193,878 users). The meta-learners use LightGBM and the known propensity, trained on 4,000,001 users; the causal forest got 500,000 because it is far slower. The winner is picked on validation Qini, and everything below is on the test set with 200-replicate Poisson bootstrap CIs.

Conversions are harder. The base rate is 0.29% and the effect about 0.1 pp, so each user carries roughly a tenth of the signal of a visit. I didn't re-weight classes, because the CATE is a difference of two probabilities and re-weighting distorts both. Besides training conversion models directly, I scored the visit-trained models against conversions, since a dense related outcome can rank better than the rare one. Validation picked a visit-trained model, but none of them separates from the response model.

7. Targeting under a budget¶

Incremental outcomes per 1,000,000 users, estimated on the test set as the mean doubly robust score of the targeted users (nuisance models fit on the training split), so the numbers hold up despite the imbalance in section 3.

Outcome Budget Uplift model Response model Random Share of all extra
visit 10% 6,012 [5,672, 6,352] 5,082 [4,688, 5,476] 758 [712, 804] 79%
visit 20% 6,892 [6,500, 7,284] 6,797 [6,358, 7,236] 1,516 [1,423, 1,608] 91%
visit 30% 7,007 [6,600, 7,414] 7,216 [6,764, 7,667] 2,273 [2,135, 2,412] 92%
visit 50% 7,231 [6,814, 7,648] 7,461 [7,002, 7,921] 3,789 [3,558, 4,020] 95%
conversion 10% 810 [700, 919] 890 [771, 1,008] 99 [87, 112] 82%
conversion 20% 908 [790, 1,026] 943 [820, 1,065] 198 [173, 223] 92%
conversion 30% 932 [811, 1,052] 955 [831, 1,079] 297 [260, 335] 94%
conversion 50% 951 [829, 1,074] 975 [850, 1,100] 496 [433, 559] 96%

A response model loses only when the budget is tight. Its top 10% would visit at 32.5% without any ad, against 21.3% for the uplift model's top 10%. From 20% upwards the two are indistinguishable: uplift in this data sits mostly with high-propensity users, so propensity alone is a decent proxy (rank correlation 0.76, 63% of the top deciles shared). I expected a bigger win for the uplift model than this.

I also looked for users the ads hurt, with thresholds fixed on validation. The 5.1% predicted to be harmed show a positive effect on test (0.43 pp [0.07, 0.79]), so the negative predictions are noise. The useful segment is the opposite one: the half of users with the lowest predicted uplift, who produce about 5% of the extra visits.

8. Where things disagree or mislead¶

All five learners agree that uplift tracks baseline propensity, but they order users differently within it (prediction SD in pp: S-learner 2.24, T-learner 2.91, X-learner 2.25, DR-learner 2.39, Causal forest 1.76). The T-learner is the odd one out. Its control model sees only 15% of the data, so its predictions are the most spread out and its calibration slope the flattest. The X-learner was built for exactly this imbalance, and the S-learner did better than I expected, probably because the effect scales with the baseline. DR and the causal forest over-predict a little where the true effect is near zero. The 10% of users with the most disagreement have a 14.4% baseline (against 2.6%) and a distinct feature profile.

Things that looked fine and weren't:

  1. The randomization checks. They pass, yet the raw ATE ends up 38% too high for visits and 16% for conversions.
  2. The average lift. The top decile of predicted uplift accounts for 84% of incremental visits and the bottom half for 2%.
  3. Exposed users. They visit far more, mostly because of who they are.
  4. Relative lift on conversions. +59% sounds big, but it is 0.115 pp, about 1,152 extra conversions per million users.
  5. Storage order. The CSV is sorted by treatment, and tied model scores inherited that order in decile tables until ties were broken at random.

9. Checking the methods on synthetic data¶

The same code runs on synthetic data shaped like Criteo's (12 features, 85/15 assignment, exposure only for the treated, heterogeneous effects including a negative pocket), where the answers are known. Every ATE estimator's CI covered the true value (5.197 pp). Over 300 replications the CIs covered 92.3% (difference in means) and 93.0% (CUPED) of the time, slightly under 95%. The CUPED bias was -0.089 pp (MC SE 0.066). On synthetic A/A data the mSPRT's false-positive rate was 0.2%, against 37.5% for peeking.

10. Limitations¶

  • The public file was re-sampled on the outcome on purpose, so absolute effects describe this file, not Criteo's campaigns. AIPW fixes the covariate-dependent assignment that causes, but no adjustment undoes selection on the outcome.
  • Without the sub-test identifier I can't analyse each test separately, which is what I'd really want.
  • The causal forest trained on 8x less data than the other learners.
  • Conversion uplift is close to the noise floor.
  • The mSPRT relies on a normal approximation that is rough at the first few conversion looks.
